source_title: Why some hugs stay with us for years, according to study of 15,000 adults
source_excerpt: Think about a hug you still remember, even though it happened years ago. It may have come from a parent when you were upset, a friend who knew you were struggling, or someone you had not seen in a long time. You may not remember exactly where you were standing or how long the embrace lasted. But you remember how you felt afterwards.A new study suggests that this emotional response may be what makes certain hugs stay in our memories. Researchers from the University of Bristol and other institutions found that people were more likely to remember a hug because it made them feel comforted, supported or understood than because of the physical gesture itself.The research, published in the journal PLOS One, analysed responses from 15,049 adults in the UK. It examined whether people remembered a hug for its positive emotional impact and whether personality and individual differences were associated with these memories. Nearly seven in 10 participants, 69.5% said they could recall a hug that had a positive emotional effect on them.What makes a hug memorable?The researchers found that comfort was the most commonly selected reason for remembering a hug. Other reasons included feeling supported, understood, happy or connected to someone. This suggests that a hug can become meaningful because of what it communicates at a particular moment. When someone embraces us during a difficult period, the gesture may convey reassurance without requiring an explanation. A hug after a long separation may communicate affection, while one offered during grief may make a person feel that they are not facing the situation alone.The researchers also examined whether individual characteristics could help explain why some people remembered these experiences more strongly than others. People who scored higher on measures of empathy and awareness of their bodily experiences were more likely to recall an emotionally meaningful hug. Those who were less comfortable with emotional closeness, measured through attachment-related avoidance, were less likely to report such memories.The study also found differences between men and women in the reasons they remembered particular hugs. Women were more likely to identify comfort as the reason, while men were more likely to report physical arousal, friendliness or understanding. These differences were relatively small and should not be treated as fixed rules about how men and women experience affection.Why do some people remember these moments more strongly?The findings suggest that memories of physical affection are not shaped by touch alone. The relationship between the people involved, the emotional situation and an individual's comfort with closeness may all influence how the experience is remembered.For instance, a hug from someone who has been emotionally supportive may carry a different meaning from an otherwise similar hug from an acquaintance. The physical action may look the same, but the personal significance can be very different.The researchers also considered attachment styles, which describe patterns in how people experience closeness and relationships. People with higher attachment-related avoidance may be less comfortable depending on others or expressing emotional closeness. This could partly explain why they were less likely to recall a hug for its positive emotional impact.However, the study does not establish that attachment style causes people to remember or forget particular hugs. It identifies associations between reported characteristics and memories.What the research cannot tell usThe study offers an interesting look at how adults remember affectionate touch, but it has limitations. Participants were asked to recall their own experiences, so the findings depend on personal memory and self-reported responses.The sample was also drawn from the UK, and women made up around 75% of participants. The researchers caution that the findings may not apply in the same way to cultures where attitudes towards physical contact and personal space are different.The research was based on survey data and cannot establish cause and effect. It cannot prove that a particular kind of hug creates a lasting memory or that everyone experiences physical affection in the same way. Still, the findings offer a useful way to think about why some ordinary gestures remain important long after the moment has passed. A hug may last only a few seconds, but the feeling of being understood, reassured or supported can become part of how a person remembers that time in their life.You use AI every day.
